I am a fourth-year Economics PhD student at the University of Minnesota, and a Research Analyst at the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis.
My research interests are broadly in Macro-Finance, with a current focus on financial intermediation, the industrial organization of banking and financial markets, and how central bank facilities interact with the financial sector.
Previously, I have worked for the Bank of England (where I was a Graduate Research Intern in Summer 2025), as well as the Federal Reserve Board (where I was a Graduate Research Intern in Summer 2024, and before that a Research Assistant).

title: Ethan Cohen
text:
Beyond Reserves: The Federal Reserve’s Balance Sheet and the Repo Market


with Sriya Anbil (Fed), Alyssa Anderson (Fed), and Romina Ruprecht (Fed)


[FEDS Working Paper] [SSRN]


Revise and Resubmit at The Journal of Finance



Abstract

We present a new constraint on the size of the Fed’s balance sheet: the supply of money held by non-banks. Calibrating a structural model to the recent monetary tightening cycle, we show that this new constraint implies a larger Federal Reserve balance sheet with more short-term liquidity provision than a balance sheet that considers only bank reserve demand. We argue that ignoring the supply of money held by non-banks could lead to loss of interest rate control by the Federal Reserve.




Monetary Policy Transmission with Endogenous Reserve Supply


with Kristina Bluwstein (BoE), Michael McLeay (BoE), and Jacob Stevens (BoE)


(Draft available upon request) [Slides]



Abstract

The Bank of England is currently transitioning from a supply-driven to a demand-driven reserves framework, where most reserves will be borrowed by banks through repurchase agreements. We build a structural model of the UK financial system with rich interactions between banks and non-bank financial institutions to study how this framework shift affects conventional and unconventional monetary policy transmission. Calibrated to the current quantitative tightening cycle, the model endogenously produces terminal central bank balance sheet sizes within current estimates of the Preferred Minimum Range of Reserves, but suggests that reaching its lower end could generate pressure in secured markets. Conservatively, steady-state reserve balances around £550 billion minimize such pressures. Our quantitative simulations deliver a rule of thumb: each £50 billion reduction in gilt holdings by the central bank raises the secured rate by about 3 basis points and lowers equilibrium reserves by roughly £20 billion.

text:
Two kinds of evidence ship with the repository: validation scripts that demonstrate each execution mode solving problems a local optimizer fails on, and a benchmark against other Julia global-optimization packages. Both are runnable, assert their claims, and exit with an error if a claim fails.

Demonstrates

compare_global_optimizers.jl runs both TikTak variants and eight competitors on five problems — Griewank-2D, Levy-4D, Rosenbrock-4D, Rastrigin-4D and -6D — under equal evaluation budgets (20k–60k). Design choices that matter for fairness:

every function is shifted off-center by a seeded draw (otherwise center-sampling methods get Rastrigin’s origin-minimum for free);

evaluations are counted by wrapping the objective; exceeding the budget is flagged rather than silently accepted;
stochastic solvers report the median of 3 seeds; TikTak and DIRECT are deterministic.

Total evals is the sum of the per-problem median evaluation counts. Total time is wall-clock time spent by the benchmark script for that row, so stochastic solvers include all three seeds. These timings are a sample run; evaluation counts are the stable budget measure.
Reading the table honestly:

TikTak.jl (BOBYQA) is the only solver at 5/5 within budget, and it used 73,407 evaluations across the suite vs 200,010 for BlackBoxOptim, the other 5/5 solver. That is about 63% fewer objective calls.
MultistartOptimization.jl (the other Julia TikTak) solves 4/5 at the median and exceeds the budget on 4 of 5 problems — up to 6.1× on Rosenbrock — because its local-search phase has no overall evaluation cap.
TikTak.jl (Nelder-Mead) misses shifted Rastrigin at these budgets (basin capture there is a knife-edge for NM; ~1.5× more local searches fix it). This mirrors the original Fortran, whose default solver is the BOBYQA family with the simplex as the non-smooth fallback. Reach for NM when the objective is noisy, and give it budget.
CMA-ES stops early on its own stagnation criterion — single-run CMA-ES is not a multistart method; restart wrappers would score better.

Caveats: this is a smoke-level comparison in the spirit of the AGK benchmarking exercise, not a publication-grade study — one shift per problem, 3 seeds, competitor defaults except budget caps. It is designed to answer a narrow question: which solver gets reliable answers under a fixed evaluation budget? BlackBoxOptim runs unseeded because its fixed-seed code path crashes on modern Julia (v0.6.5).
Run it yourself (first run installs competitor packages into a self-managed, git-ignored environment):
julia examples/benchmarks/compare_global_optimizers.jl

For your own experiments:

griewank(x)   = sum(abs2, x)/200 - prod(cos(x[i]/sqrt(i)) for i in eachindex(x)) + 1  # [-100, 100]ⁿ
rosenbrock(x) = sum(100*(x[i+1]-x[i]^2)^2 + (1-x[i])^2 for i in 1:length(x)-1)        # [-5, 10]ⁿ
function levy(x)                                                         # [-10, 10]ⁿ
    w = 1 .+ (x .- 1) ./ 4
    sin(pi*w[1])^2 +
        sum((w[i]-1)^2 * (1 + 10sin(pi*w[i]+1)^2) for i in 1:length(x)-1) +
        (w[end]-1)^2 * (1 + sin(2pi*w[end])^2)

title: Basic Usage
text:
Worked examples, smallest first. All runnable as written.


using TikTak

f(x) = sum((x .- [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]).^2)

result = tiktak(f, fill(-10.0, 3), fill(10.0, 3))
result.minimizer   # ≈ [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]



rastrigin(x) = 10length(x) + sum(xi^2 - 10cos(2pi * xi) for xi in x)

lower, upper = fill(-5.12, 4), fill(5.12, 4)

# Defaults are sized for easier problems:
r1 = tiktak(rastrigin, lower, upper)

# Rugged surfaces want more seeds and searches, and a smooth objective
# is BOBYQA territory:
r2 = tiktak(rastrigin, lower, upper;
            options = TikTakOptions(n_sobol = 4000, n_local = 100,
                                    local_optimizer = BOBYQA()))
r2.minimum   # 0.0, at ~13k evaluations



r_first = tiktak(f, lower, upper)

# later, after changing the data or tightening tolerances:
r_second = tiktak(f, lower, upper; x0 = r_first.minimizer)
x0 joins the seed pool as a candidate — if it is good, early searches mix toward it immediately.



# Hard bounds keep the model solvable; the prior says the answer is central.
result = tiktak(f, fill(-10.0, 4), fill(10.0, 4);
                sobol_lower = fill(-2.0, 4),
                sobol_upper = fill( 2.0, 4))
Seeds concentrate where you expect the optimum; local searches may still leave the sampling region (they respect only the hard bounds).



function fragile(x)
    x[1] < 0 && error("model failed to converge")
    return sum(abs2, x)
end

result = tiktak(fragile, [-5.0, -5.0], [5.0, 5.0];
                options = TikTakOptions(catch_errors = true, fval_max = 1e8))
Failures evaluate to fval_max (the Fortran penalty convention) instead of killing the run. Choose a finite penalty that is worse than any plausible successful value, so failed draws sink to the bottom of the candidate list.



using Random
opts = TikTakOptions(search_type = :lottery, n_lottery = 10,
                     rng = MersenneTwister(42))
result = tiktak(rastrigin, lower, upper; options = opts)
Instead of always mixing toward the single best result, each search draws its base point from the top n_lottery completed results (probability ∝ 1/rank) — more exploration on surfaces with several competitive basins, at the cost of determinism (seed the rng to reproduce).



# Noisy objective: finite-difference BFGS gradients would be garbage,
# polish with a tight simplex instead
opts = TikTakOptions(final_polish_optimizer =
                         NelderMead(tol = 1e-8, maxiter = 2000,
                                    initial_simplex_scale = 0.01))

# Or skip polishing entirely
opts = TikTakOptions(final_polish = false)
The default polish is BFGS (as in the Fortran), and it is accepted only when it improves the incumbent — on a noisy objective it can waste evaluations but cannot make the answer worse.



result = tiktak(rastrigin, lower, upper;
                options = TikTakOptions(n_sobol = 1000, n_local = 40))

best_seed = minimum(last, result.sobol_results)   # best raw Sobol value
result.minimum                                    # after local searches + polish

# How many distinct local minima did the searches find?
vals = sort(unique(round.(last.(result.local_results), digits = 6)))
A big gap between the best seed and the final minimum, or many distinct local-search values, are both signs the surface is rugged and the budget deserves a second look — see Convergence Properties.

r_first = tiktak(f, lower, upper)

# later, after changing the data or tightening tolerances:
r_second = tiktak(f, lower, upper; x0 = r_first.minimizer)
x0 joins the seed pool as a candidate — if it is good, early searches mix toward it immediately.

title: Basic Usage
text:
# Hard bounds keep the model solvable; the prior says the answer is central.
result = tiktak(f, fill(-10.0, 4), fill(10.0, 4);
                sobol_lower = fill(-2.0, 4),
                sobol_upper = fill( 2.0, 4))
Seeds concentrate where you expect the optimum; local searches may still leave the sampling region (they respect only the hard bounds).

title: Basic Usage
Basic Usage
text:
using Random
opts = TikTakOptions(search_type = :lottery, n_lottery = 10,
                     rng = MersenneTwister(42))
result = tiktak(rastrigin, lower, upper; options = opts)
Instead of always mixing toward the single best result, each search draws its base point from the top n_lottery completed results (probability ∝ 1/rank) — more exploration on surfaces with several competitive basins, at the cost of determinism (seed the rng to reproduce).

title: Basic Usage
text:
# Noisy objective: finite-difference BFGS gradients would be garbage,
# polish with a tight simplex instead
opts = TikTakOptions(final_polish_optimizer =
                         NelderMead(tol = 1e-8, maxiter = 2000,
                                    initial_simplex_scale = 0.01))

# Or skip polishing entirely
opts = TikTakOptions(final_polish = false)
The default polish is BFGS (as in the Fortran), and it is accepted only when it improves the incumbent — on a noisy objective it can waste evaluations but cannot make the answer worse.

title: Basic Usage
text:
result = tiktak(rastrigin, lower, upper;
                options = TikTakOptions(n_sobol = 1000, n_local = 40))

best_seed = minimum(last, result.sobol_results)   # best raw Sobol value
result.minimum                                    # after local searches + polish

# How many distinct local minima did the searches find?
vals = sort(unique(round.(last.(result.local_results), digits = 6)))
A big gap between the best seed and the final minimum, or many distinct local-search values, are both signs the surface is rugged and the budget deserves a second look — see Convergence Properties.

title: Convergence Properties
text:
Honest answers about what TikTak does and does not guarantee.



Asymptotic coverage. Sobol’ sequences are dense in the box: as n_sobol → ∞, some seed falls inside the global basin, and the local search started (nearly) at that seed converges to the global minimum. This is the standard multistart guarantee — real, but asymptotic; it says nothing about a finite budget.
Local convergence. Each phase-2 search inherits the convergence theory of its local optimizer (Nelder–Mead’s practical convergence on well-behaved functions, BOBYQA’s and L-BFGS’s theory on smooth ones, LM’s on least squares).
Monotone incumbent. The reported minimum is the best of all phase-1 points, all phase-2 results, and the polish: it never moves up, and the polish is accepted only if it improves.

There is no finite-time guarantee of finding the global minimum — that is true of every practical global optimizer on black-box objectives. What the algorithm offers is an evaluation-efficient allocation of a finite budget, and the empirical record (the AGK 2022 study, and this package’s benchmarks) that the allocation works.



The failure mode is basin miss: no kept seed (and no mixed starting point) lands in the global basin, so every search refines some other valley. The result is a clean convergence to the wrong answer — there is no warning sign in the optimizer output itself. On shifted Rastrigin-4D, whose global basin occupies ~1e-4 of the box, our Nelder–Mead configuration at the benchmark budget lands one basin off (f = 0.995) while BOBYQA captures it; 1.5× more local searches fix the NM run. Capture is a budget knife-edge, not a property of the algorithm.




Gap between phases. Compare minimum(last.(result.sobol_results)) with result.minimum. A large improvement from local searches with many distinct terminal values suggests a rugged surface — consider more n_sobol/n_local.
Distinct local minima. Cluster result.local_results values: if the best value is achieved by a single search while others scatter widely, treat the result with suspicion and increase the budget.
Budget doubling. The cheapest credible check: rerun with double n_sobol (Sobol points are extensible — the first half is the same sequence) and confirm the minimizer is stable.
Sampling region. If you can bound the plausible region, sample seeds there (sobol_lower/sobol_upper) — coverage of the region that matters improves at no extra cost.
The paper’s stopping heuristic. AGK suggest stopping when the last two distinct incumbent values are sufficiently close. With this package, run with a budget, inspect, and warm-start a second run via x0 if needed.




Serial tiktak with search_type = :best is deterministic, so a result can be reproduced exactly, bisected over options, and compared across code changes. Use the deterministic serial mode for final reported estimates; use the parallel modes (whose incumbent-update order is timing-dependent) for exploration at scale.

title: Algorithm Overview
text:
TikTak is a multistart global optimization algorithm: quasi-random exploration first, then a schedule of local searches that are pulled increasingly toward the best solution found so far. It was developed for structural estimation problems — expensive objectives, many local minima, noisy or kinked surfaces — and benchmarked against other global optimizers in Arnoud, Guvenen & Kleineberg (2022).
This implementation follows the reference Fortran code (TiktakGlobalSearch.f90 by Guvenen & Ozkan). Every default below is the Fortran default unless explicitly marked otherwise.


Draw n_sobol points from a Sobol sequence scaled to the sampling region and evaluate the objective at each. Keep the best n_local points, sorted by objective value, as seeds. The rest are discarded — their neighborhoods looked unpromising.
Why Sobol rather than random? Low-discrepancy sequences cover the box evenly with no clusters or gaps, so the same number of points buys strictly better coverage of basins; and the sequence is deterministic, which makes runs reproducible.
Two refinements, both from the original:

Sampling region vs bounds. Pass sobol_lower/sobol_upper to sample seeds in a tighter plausible region while local searches respect the full bounds (Fortran p_range vs p_bound).
Legitimacy early stop. With n_legitimate = m and fval_max = c, phase 1 stops as soon as m points with f(x) < c have been found — useful when much of the box makes the model fail and you only need enough viable seeds.




For search j = 1, \dots, N^* (seeds s_{(j)} sorted best-first), the starting point is a convex combination of the next seed and the best point found so far Z^*_{j-1}:
\tilde{x}_j = \theta_j \, Z^*_{j-1} + (1 - \theta_j) \, s_{(j)},
\qquad
\theta_j = \operatorname{clamp}\!\left(\sqrt{j / N^*},\; \theta_{\min},\; \theta_{\max}\right)
Early searches start almost exactly at their (diverse) seeds — exploration. Late searches start almost on top of the incumbent — exploitation, refining the best basin from slightly different angles.
Defaults: \theta_{\min} = 0.1, \theta_{\max} = 0.95. The cap follows the reference Fortran; the AGK (2022) paper states 0.995. Both are reasonable — set TikTakOptions(theta_max = 0.995) to follow the paper.
A local optimizer then runs from \tilde{x}_j, with per-iteration configuration that follows the Fortran schedules:

Nelder–Mead: constant initial simplex scale 1 / (N^*)^{1/n} of each parameter’s range (the runAmoeba rule), relative f-tolerance 1e-4 (p_tolf_amoeba). An explicitly set initial_simplex_scale is used as-is.
BOBYQA: initial trust radius 0.4 × the minimum range (min_range / 2.5), final radius 1e-3; once j/N^* > 0.5 both shrink by 1/(4 \, j/N^*) — later searches are local refinements, not basin hops.
BFGS / LevenbergMarquardt: passed through unchanged.

With search_type = :lottery, the base point is drawn from the top n_lottery completed results with probability proportional to the inverse rank, instead of always using the single best.



One last search from the overall best point, by default with BFGS (quasi-Newton with finite-difference gradients) — exactly what the Fortran’s lastSearch does with DFPMIN. The polish result is accepted only if it improves, so a failed polish on a noisy objective costs evaluations but cannot worsen the answer. Override with final_polish_optimizer, or disable with final_polish = false.



Random multistart wastes most searches re-discovering the same mediocre basins. TikTak (i) starts only from the best fraction of an evenly-covering Sobol scan, and (ii) reuses information across searches through the mixing schedule — late searches concentrate evaluations where the evidence points. On Rastrigin-4D, 100 random Nelder–Mead restarts end at f ≈ 1–3 in 10 of 10 seeds, while TikTak with the same number of local searches finds the exact global minimum, using fewer total evaluations (examples/validation/serial.jl).

title: Distributed
text:
Multi-process parallelism with tiktak_parallel, built on Distributed.jl. Workers are separate OS processes, so the objective does not need to be thread-safe — each process has its own globals and buffers.


using Distributed
addprocs(8)                      # local processes; see below for remote

@everywhere using TikTak
@everywhere function f(x)        # the objective MUST exist on every worker
    return (1 - x[1])^2 + 100 * (x[2] - x[1]^2)^2
end

result = tiktak_parallel(f, [-5.0, -5.0], [5.0, 5.0];
                         options = TikTakOptions(n_sobol = 4000, n_local = 100))
The coordinator hands out Sobol points and local searches to workers as they free up (dynamic load balancing), keeps the incumbent under a lock, and runs the final polish itself.
Common pitfalls:

UndefVarError on a worker → the objective (or data it closes over) was not defined with @everywhere. Define functions and load data on all processes.
Large data → load it on each worker (e.g. @everywhere data = load(...)) rather than capturing it in a closure, which would be serialized with every call.
Use worker_ids = [...] to restrict which workers participate.




addprocs([("user@node1", 4), ("user@node2", 4)])   # SSH
# or inside a Slurm allocation:
# using ClusterManagers; addprocs_slurm(64)
Everything else is unchanged. Note this mode has no crash recovery: if a worker dies, Distributed raises an error on the coordinator. For long runs, save your model outputs and restart a new TikTak run from the best point with x0.



examples/validation/distributed.jl spawns 4 workers, solves Rastrigin-4D with a synthetic objective, and checks that the distributed result matches the serial one. The test suite additionally runs a 2-worker distributed solve, including lottery mode, on every CI run.

title: Parallelization Overview
text:
TikTak has two expensive phases: evaluating Sobol points and running local searches. Both phases parallelize naturally because each objective evaluation is independent once its starting point has been chosen.
This release supports three execution modes:



Mode
Function
Execution model
Best for




Serial
tiktak
one Julia process
debugging, reproducible baseline runs


Threaded
tiktak_threaded
one process, many threads
a laptop or workstation with thread-safe model code


Distributed
tiktak_parallel
multiple Distributed.jl workers
process isolation or a small cluster allocation





Use tiktak first while you are checking bounds, penalties, and optimizer settings. It is the easiest result to reason about.
Use tiktak_threaded when your objective is thread-safe: no shared mutable buffers, no writes to the same files, and no libraries that assume single threaded use.
Use tiktak_parallel when process isolation is cleaner than threads, or when you already have a Distributed.jl worker pool. The objective function must be available on every worker.



Parallel speedup depends on how expensive the objective is. For cheap toy functions, scheduling overhead and the final polish can dominate. For the calibration problems TikTak was designed for, where each evaluation can take seconds or minutes, the Sobol phase and the local searches usually keep workers busy.
The threaded and distributed paths are asynchronous in the ordinary sense: workers start local searches as soon as they are assigned work. A search reads the current best point at the moment it starts, so parallel runs can differ slightly from serial runs and from each other. That is expected.



The runnable validation scripts live in examples/validation/:

serial.jl checks the baseline algorithm on a multimodal benchmark.
threaded.jl checks the shared-memory path.
distributed.jl checks the Distributed.jl path.

The file-coordinated PBS/Slurm mode from the reference implementation is not part of this release. It is better to ship a smaller package than to promise a cluster workflow that has not been exercised on a real cluster yet.

title: Threading
text:
Shared-memory parallelism with tiktak_threaded. Simplest parallel mode: no process setup, no data movement.


julia -t 8           # or: julia -t auto
using TikTak

result = tiktak_threaded(f, lower, upper;
                         options = TikTakOptions(n_sobol = 4000, n_local = 100))
Both phases are threaded: Sobol evaluations are distributed across threads, and local searches run concurrently with the incumbent guarded by a lock. All tiktak keywords (x0, sobol_lower/sobol_upper) work unchanged.



The objective is called concurrently from many threads. Safe:
# Pure function of x — allocates its own workspace
function f(x)
    model = solve_model(x)          # local state only
    return distance(model, data)
end
Unsafe — shared mutable workspace:
const workspace = zeros(1000)       # DON'T: shared buffer
function f(x)
    solve_model!(workspace, x)      # data race across threads
    return distance(workspace, data)
end
If your model code needs preallocated buffers, allocate per call, or keep one workspace per thread and index it by Threads.threadid() only if your Julia version pins tasks to threads for the whole call (safer: per-call allocation or a Channel of workspaces).
Also beware: global RNG use inside the objective makes results timing-dependent; file output from inside the objective needs its own locking.



examples/validation/threaded.jl (run with julia --project=. -t 4 ...) checks that the threaded mode finds the Rastrigin-4D global minimum the serial mode finds, that lottery mode works, and that the run is faster than serial on a cheap synthetic objective. Treat that as a smoke test, not a promise about your model: speedup improves as each objective evaluation gets more expensive.




Objective not thread-safe and not easily made so → use Distributed (process isolation).
Need more cores than one machine → use Distributed, or run multiple independent Julia workers from your scheduler.
Jobs may be preempted/killed mid-run → checkpoint your own model state and restart the optimization from the best point with x0.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
Real failure modes and what they mean, roughly in the order you might meet them.


Set TikTakOptions(catch_errors = true, fval_max = 1e8). Exceptions and non-finite values then evaluate to fval_max (the Fortran penalty convention), so the run keeps going and failed draws sort behind real candidates. Prefer a finite fval_max: it doubles as the legitimacy threshold and keeps comparisons well-defined.



NLopt reported a setup-level problem or a forced stop. Check that the bounds are finite and ordered, that the objective returns finite numbers in the region you gave TikTak, and that custom stopping logic is not firing unexpectedly.
TikTak does not warn on every NLopt non-success code. title: Mathematical Details
text:
Formal statement of the algorithm as implemented (matching the reference Fortran; see the fidelity table).


\min_{x \in [\ell, u] \subset \mathbb{R}^n} f(x)
with f available only through (possibly expensive, noisy, non-smooth) point evaluations. Optionally a sampling region [\ell_s, u_s] \subseteq [\ell, u] restricts where seeds are drawn.



Let \{q_i\}_{i=1}^{N} be consecutive points of the n-dimensional Sobol’ sequence (the all-zeros initial point is skipped, as in the Fortran’s insobl). Seeds are evaluated at
x_i = \ell_s + q_i \odot (u_s - \ell_s), \qquad f_i = f(x_i),
and the best N^* (sorted ascending, duplicates by index removed) become seeds s_{(1)}, \dots, s_{(N^*)} with f(s_{(1)}) \le \dots \le f(s_{(N^*)}).
Legitimacy early stop. Given a threshold c (fval_max) and target m (n_legitimate), phase 1 terminates at the first index k such that \#\{i \le k : f_i < c\} = m.



For j = 1, \dots, N^*, with incumbent Z^*_{j-1} = \arg\min over all completed local-search results (initialized to the best seed):
\theta_j = \operatorname{clamp}\!\left(\sqrt{\tfrac{j}{N^*}},\,
            \theta_{\min},\, \theta_{\max}\right),
\qquad
\tilde{x}_j = \operatorname{clamp}\!\left(
  \theta_j Z^*_{j-1} + (1-\theta_j)\, s_{(j)},\, \ell,\, u\right),
followed by a bound-constrained local search from \tilde{x}_j. Defaults \theta_{\min} = 0.1, \theta_{\max} = 0.95 (Fortran; the paper states 0.995).
Properties of the schedule: \theta_j is nondecreasing, hits the lower clamp for j \le \theta_{\min}^2 N^* (the first 1% of searches at the default) and the upper clamp for j \ge \theta_{\max}^2 N^* (the last ~10%). Because s_{(1)} initializes the incumbent, the first search starts exactly at the best seed regardless of \theta_1.
Lottery variant. With search_type = :lottery, the base point replaces Z^*_{j-1} by a draw from the K best completed results (K = n_lottery) with rank-based probabilities
P(\text{rank } i) = \frac{1/i}{\sum_{k=1}^{K} 1/k}, \qquad i = 1, \dots, K.



With r = u - \ell and t_j = j/N^*:

Nelder–Mead (amoeba analog): initial simplex step in coordinate k is \sigma \, r_k with \sigma = \min\{0.5,\, (N^*)^{-1/n}\} (constant in j); stops when the relative spread of simplex values 2|f_{\max}-f_{\min}|/(|f_{\max}|+|f_{\min}|) falls below tol (default 10^{-4}), with tol·10^{-3} as an absolute backstop.
BOBYQA (bobyqa_h analog, scalar): trust radii
(\rho_{\text{beg}}, \rho_{\text{end}})_j =
\begin{cases}
(0.4\,\min_k r_k,\; 10^{-3}) & t_j \le 0.5\\[2pt]
\left(\dfrac{0.4\,\min_k r_k}{4 t_j},\; \dfrac{10^{-3}}{4 t_j}\right) & t_j > 0.5
\end{cases}
with \rho_{\text{end}} enforced as an absolute x-space tolerance.
BFGS: L-BFGS with central finite differences, h_k = \varepsilon^{1/3} \max(|x_k|, 1), one-sided at active bounds.
Levenberg–Marquardt (for f(x) = \|r(x)\|^2): forward-difference Jacobian J; damped step \delta solves
\left(J^\top J + \lambda \, \operatorname{diag}(J^\top J)\right) \delta
= -J^\top r,
with \lambda decreased by 3 on success and grown geometrically on failure; trial points are clamped to the box; failed residual evaluations reject the step. Stops on step size, relative cost decrease, or \|J^\top r\|_\infty.




x^{\text{final}} = \operatorname{LocalSearch}_{\text{BFGS}}\!\left(Z^*_{N^*}\right),
accepted only if it improves on Z^*_{N^*}.



Total objective evaluations are approximately
N \;+\; \sum_{j=1}^{N^*} E_j \;+\; E_{\text{polish}},
where E_j is the per-search evaluation count (bounded by maxiter; for LM roughly (n+1) \times iterations). At the package defaults the Sobol phase dominates for cheap-to-moderate local searches; the benchmarks report measured totals of roughly 0.3\text{–}0.6 \times the nominal budget across the suite.



The Sobol sequence is deterministic and search_type = :best introduces no randomness, so serial runs are exactly reproducible given the same options. Lottery mode consumes draws from options.rng. Parallel modes evaluate the same point sets, but the incumbent’s update order depends on completion timing, which can change which basin a mid-schedule search refines.

title: TikTak.jl
text:
Global optimization for expensive, multimodal objectives — a Julia implementation of the TikTak algorithm, faithful to the reference Fortran implementation by Guvenen and coauthors.


TikTak is a multistart global optimization algorithm described in Arnoud, Guvenen & Kleineberg (2022), Benchmarking Global Optimizers, and used to estimate structural economic models whose objectives are expensive to evaluate, non-smooth, and riddled with local minima.
The algorithm runs in two phases plus a polish:

Sobol pre-testing — evaluate the objective at N quasi-random Sobol points and keep the best N^* as seeds.
Local searches — run N^* local optimizations, each started from a convex combination of the next seed and the best minimum found so far. The mixing weight \theta_j grows over the schedule, shifting effort from exploration to exploitation.
Final polish — a quasi-Newton (BFGS) search from the overall best point.





Faithful to the reference implementation. Defaults — the mixing-weight schedule, local-search tolerances, trust-region shrinkage, the BFGS final polish — match the original Fortran (TiktakGlobalSearch.f90), with every deliberate deviation documented. See Algorithm Overview.
Four local optimizers: Nelder–Mead, BOBYQA, finite-difference BFGS, and a least-squares Levenberg–Marquardt solver that exploits the residual structure of MSM/GMM objectives via ResidualObjective — the role the original’s default DFNLS solver plays. See Local Optimizers.
Three execution modes: serial, multithreaded, and Distributed.jl multi-process. See Parallelization.
Validated and benchmarked. The test suite covers serial, threaded, and distributed execution, and the examples include a benchmark against other Julia global optimizers (see below).




Five shifted multimodal problems (Griewank, Levy, Rosenbrock, Rastrigin in 2–6 dimensions), equal evaluation budgets, success threshold f < 1e-4 (all global minima are 0). Full details and caveats in Benchmarks & Validation.
The main result: TikTak.jl (BOBYQA) is the only solver that solves all five problems within budget, using about 37% of BlackBoxOptim’s objective evaluations.

title: MSM Calibration
text:
TikTak’s home turf: estimating structural parameters by Method of Simulated Moments. The objective is a weighted distance between simulated and data moments — expensive (every evaluation solves and simulates the model), multimodal, and possibly noisy.


The MSM criterion
f(\theta) = \left(\hat{m}(\theta) - m\right)' W \left(\hat{m}(\theta) - m\right)
is a sum of squares: with W = C'C (Cholesky), define the residual vector r(\theta) = C\,(\hat{m}(\theta) - m) so that f = \|r\|^2. This is exactly the original Fortran’s design — the user supplies the residual vector (dfovec), and the default solver exploits the least-squares structure. In this package that role is played by ResidualObjective + LevenbergMarquardt:
using TikTak, LinearAlgebra

data_moments = [0.31, 0.58, 0.12, 0.044, 0.27]
W = Diagonal(1 ./ abs2.(data_moments))      # proportional weighting
C = cholesky(Matrix(W)).U

function simulated_moments(θ)
    # solve the model at θ and compute the same 5 moments from the simulation
    ...
end

residuals(θ) = C * (simulated_moments(θ) .- data_moments)
f = ResidualObjective(residuals)            # f(θ) = ‖r(θ)‖²

lower = [0.90, 0.0, 0.01, 0.5, 0.0]         # e.g. [β, ρ, σ, γ, λ]
upper = [0.999, 0.99, 0.50, 5.0, 1.0]

opts = TikTakOptions(
    n_sobol = 2000,
    n_local = 100,
    local_optimizer = LevenbergMarquardt(),
    catch_errors = true,                    # failed model solves → penalty
    fval_max = 1e8,
)

result = tiktak(f, lower, upper; options = opts)
θ̂ = result.minimizer
Why bother with the residual form? On Rosenbrock-as-residuals the LM solver reaches the optimum in 674 evaluations where Nelder–Mead needs 2417 (examples/validation/serial.jl) — and each “evaluation” is a full model solve. The Jacobian costs n residual evaluations per LM iteration, which the structure-aware step more than repays on smooth problems.
When the simulated moments are noisy (finite simulated sample, chattering discrete choices), finite-difference Jacobians degrade: fix the simulation seed inside simulated_moments (common random numbers) so the objective is deterministic in θ, or fall back to NelderMead().




Bounds vs sampling region. Set hard bounds where the model is solvable; pass sobol_lower/sobol_upper for the economically plausible region so seeds concentrate where the answer should be.
Failure handling. catch_errors = true with a finite fval_max; pair with n_legitimate if large parts of the box fail and you want phase 1 to stop after enough viable seeds.
Budget. n_local ≈ 25 × n_params and n_sobol ≈ 20–50 ×   n_local served well in our benchmarks; for a model taking minutes per solve, start smaller, inspect, and warm-start a refinement run via x0.
Reproducibility. Keep search_type = :best and fix the simulation seed — the entire calibration is then deterministic.




Shared memory:
# julia -t 16
result = tiktak_threaded(f, lower, upper; options = opts)
(the model code must be thread-safe — pure functions of θ, no shared buffers).
For process isolation, use tiktak_parallel with Distributed.jl workers. If you run on a scheduler, start Julia workers inside the allocation and make sure the objective and data are loaded on every process. The file-coordinated PBS/Slurm workflow from the reference implementation is intentionally not part of this release; it needs real cluster validation before it should be public.



TikTak gives you \hat\theta; MSM standard errors need the Jacobian of moments at \hat\theta and the moment covariance. Compute the Jacobian by finite differences at the solution (re-using the converged model solve), outside the optimizer.

The MSM criterion
f(\theta) = \left(\hat{m}(\theta) - m\right)' W \left(\hat{m}(\theta) - m\right)
is a sum of squares: with W = C'C (Cholesky), define the residual vector r(\theta) = C\,(\hat{m}(\theta) - m) so that f = \|r\|^2. This is exactly the original Fortran’s design — the user supplies the residual vector (dfovec), and the default solver exploits the least-squares structure. In this package that role is played by ResidualObjective + LevenbergMarquardt:
using TikTak, LinearAlgebra

data_moments = [0.31, 0.58, 0.12, 0.044, 0.27]
W = Diagonal(1 ./ abs2.(data_moments))      # proportional weighting
C = cholesky(Matrix(W)).U

function simulated_moments(θ)
    # solve the model at θ and compute the same 5 moments from the simulation
    ...
end

residuals(θ) = C * (simulated_moments(θ) .- data_moments)
f = ResidualObjective(residuals)            # f(θ) = ‖r(θ)‖²

lower = [0.90, 0.0, 0.01, 0.5, 0.0]         # e.g. [β, ρ, σ, γ, λ]
upper = [0.999, 0.99, 0.50, 5.0, 1.0]

opts = TikTakOptions(
    n_sobol = 2000,
    n_local = 100,
    local_optimizer = LevenbergMarquardt(),
    catch_errors = true,                    # failed model solves → penalty
    fval_max = 1e8,
)

result = tiktak(f, lower, upper; options = opts)
θ̂ = result.minimizer
Why bother with the residual form? On Rosenbrock-as-residuals the LM solver reaches the optimum in 674 evaluations where Nelder–Mead needs 2417 (examples/validation/serial.jl) — and each “evaluation” is a full model solve. The Jacobian costs n residual evaluations per LM iteration, which the structure-aware step more than repays on smooth problems.
When the simulated moments are noisy (finite simulated sample, chattering discrete choices), finite-difference Jacobians degrade: fix the simulation seed inside simulated_moments (common random numbers) so the objective is deterministic in θ, or fall back to NelderMead().

title: MSM Calibration
text:
Bounds vs sampling region. Set hard bounds where the model is solvable; pass sobol_lower/sobol_upper for the economically plausible region so seeds concentrate where the answer should be.
Failure handling. catch_errors = true with a finite fval_max; pair with n_legitimate if large parts of the box fail and you want phase 1 to stop after enough viable seeds.
Budget. n_local ≈ 25 × n_params and n_sobol ≈ 20–50 ×   n_local served well in our benchmarks; for a model taking minutes per solve, start smaller, inspect, and warm-start a refinement run via x0.
Reproducibility. Keep search_type = :best and fix the simulation seed — the entire calibration is then deterministic.

title: Quick Start
text:
Five minutes from using TikTak to a calibrated model.


using TikTak

rosenbrock(x) = (1 - x[1])^2 + 100 * (x[2] - x[1]^2)^2

result = tiktak(rosenbrock, [-5.0, -5.0], [5.0, 5.0])

result.minimizer        # ≈ [1.0, 1.0]
result.minimum          # ≈ 0.0
result.n_fevals         # total objective evaluations
result.n_local_searches # local searches performed (+1 for the final polish)
The two positional vectors are hard box bounds: Sobol points are sampled inside them and local searches never leave them.



opts = TikTakOptions(
    n_sobol = 4000,   # Sobol points evaluated in phase 1
    n_local = 100,    # local searches in phase 2
)
result = tiktak(rosenbrock, [-5.0, -5.0], [5.0, 5.0]; options = opts)
Rules of thumb (from the paper and our benchmarks):

n_sobol: hundreds for easy problems, thousands once local minima multiply. Scale up with dimension and ruggedness.
n_local: roughly 1–10% of n_sobol; ~25 per dimension worked well across our benchmark suite.
The defaults (1000 / 100) are a reasonable starting point for small problems; when in doubt, increase n_sobol first.




TikTakOptions(local_optimizer = NelderMead())  # default: robust to noise/kinks
TikTakOptions(local_optimizer = BOBYQA())      # faster on smooth objectives
In our benchmark, BOBYQA solved every problem within budget; Nelder–Mead needed larger budgets on the most rugged surface but is the safer choice when the objective is noisy (e.g. simulated moments with a finite number of simulated agents). The original Fortran defaults to a BOBYQA-family solver, with the simplex as its non-smooth fallback.



If your objective is a sum of squared moment deviations, say so — the Levenberg–Marquardt solver exploits that structure and typically needs several times fewer model solves:
r(x) = [model_moment(x, k) - data_moment(k) for k in 1:K]  # residual vector
f = ResidualObjective(r)                                   # f(x) = sum(abs2, r(x))

result = tiktak(f, lower, upper;
                options = TikTakOptions(local_optimizer = LevenbergMarquardt()))
See MSM Calibration for the full pattern including weighting matrices.



Model solvers crash and simulators return NaN. Tell TikTak to treat failures as penalties instead of aborting the run:
opts = TikTakOptions(catch_errors = true, fval_max = 1e8)
Any exception or non-finite value then evaluates to fval_max, mirroring the penalty convention of the original Fortran. Use a finite fval_max that is worse than any plausible successful value, so failed draws sort behind real candidates.



# Shared memory (start Julia with: julia -t 8)
result = tiktak_threaded(f, lower, upper; options = opts)

# Multiple processes
using Distributed
addprocs(8)
@everywhere using TikTak
@everywhere f(x) = ...           # objective must exist on every worker
result = tiktak_parallel(f, lower, upper; options = opts)
The file-coordinated PBS/Slurm workflow from the reference implementation is not part of this release. It needs real cluster validation before it belongs in the public API.



# Inject a known-good point as a candidate
result = tiktak(f, lower, upper; x0 = previous_estimate)

# Sample Sobol points in a tighter "plausible" region while letting local
# searches roam the full bounds (the Fortran p_range vs p_bound distinction)
result = tiktak(f, lower, upper;
                sobol_lower = plausible_lo, sobol_upper = plausible_hi)



With the default search_type = :best, a serial tiktak run is fully deterministic: Sobol points are a fixed sequence and no randomness enters the algorithm. Lottery mode (search_type = :lottery) draws from TikTakOptions(rng = ...), which you can seed. Parallel runs are deterministic in coverage (same points, same searches) but the sequence of best-so-far updates depends on completion order, so results can differ at the level of which basin a mid-schedule search lands in.
